text: On the morning of July 1st 1934, two SS men walk into a bare cell in Stadelheim prison in Munich.
One lays a loaded pistol on the table in front of the half-dressed man on the cot, then leaves.
The man is Ernst Röhm, chief of staff of the largest private army on earth — three million storm troopers.
The man who just ordered him to shoot himself is Adolf Hitler. His oldest friend of fourteen years.
Röhm looks at the pistol and refuses. If I am to be killed, he says, let Adolf do it himself.
This is the story of the weekend Hitler murdered his best friend, and hundreds of others, in seventy-two hours.
By the time it was over, Hitler would stand before parliament and call himself the supreme judge of the German people.
And the most chilling part is that the President thanked him, the Army congratulated him, and the country breathed relief.
To understand the killing, you have to understand the friendship. Röhm was there at the very beginning.
A stocky, scar-faced ex-army captain, shot through the face in the First World War, who never got over it.
It was Röhm who brought Hitler the backing of the Army and the muscle of ex-soldiers willing to crack skulls.
He built and led the S.A. — the Sturmabteilung, the brownshirts — who beat Hitler's road to power open with fists.
Hitler admitted he could not have come to power without them. And that was exactly the problem.
By 1934 Hitler was Chancellor. But the brownshirts who put him there thought the revolution had barely begun.
Röhm called it the second revolution. It terrified everyone who was not a storm trooper.
The first revolution only put Hitler in the chair. The second would sweep away the elites and the old Army.
Röhm wanted his three million brownshirts to become the new army, with himself as its commander.
To the generals of the regular Army, the Reichswehr, this was an existential threat.
Here is the trap: Hitler owed his street power to Röhm, but needed the loyalty of the professional Army.
And of the aging President, Field Marshal Hindenburg — the one man who could still remove him.
Hitler could not have both. He had to choose: his oldest friend, or the generals and the President.
Through the spring of 1934, two men made certain the choice would break their way.
Hermann Göring had traded his brown shirt for the Army caste and sided with the generals.
And Heinrich Himmler ran the black-coated S.S. — still, at this point, just a branch of Röhm's S.A.
Both understood: if Röhm fell, everything he controlled was up for grabs. So they went to work.
Himmler took the Prussian Gestapo and built a secret-police empire. Together they drew up lists of enemies to kill.
They fed Hitler rumors: that Röhm was plotting a coup, conspiring with the disgraced General von Schleicher.
Almost none of it was true. But Hitler, Shirer notes, needed little prodding to have his suspicions aroused.
Then came the ultimatum that forced his hand. Vice-Chancellor Franz von Papen found his voice.
At the University of Marburg he gave a stunning speech demanding an end to the terror and the muzzling of the press.
It fell, Shirer says, like a bombshell. Goebbels frantically tried to suppress it.
It emboldened the President. When Hitler flew to see Hindenburg, he was met by his own Defense Minister, Blomberg.
Wearing a face Hitler had never seen — stern, cold, Prussian. The message was plain.
Unless the tension ended fast, the President would declare martial law and hand the country to the Army.
That was the moment Röhm's fate was sealed. If the Army took over, Hitler was finished.
He had one way to survive: give the generals what they wanted. Destroy the S.A. Kill his oldest friend.
On June 25th the Army went on alert. On the 28th, Röhm was expelled from the Officers' League — a death sentence.
And here is the cruelest detail. Röhm had invited Hitler to a friendly S.A. conference at the lakeside resort of Bad Wiessee.
Hitler agreed. He even kept the appointment. He just didn't arrive the way Röhm expected.
Now the clock starts ticking. Thursday June 28th — Hitler is at a wedding, acting without a care.
Behind the scenes, Göring and Himmler put their S.S. detachments on standby.
Friday the 29th — Hitler arrives at a hotel on the Rhine at Godesberg. Goebbels shows up with threatening intelligence.
At one in the morning, the trigger: two urgent messages claiming the S.A. was about to rise in Berlin and Munich.
It was almost certainly a fabrication by Göring and Himmler. But it was all Hitler needed. That was mutiny, he said.
At two o'clock in the morning, he said, I flew to Munich.
At that exact moment, the men he was flying to destroy were fast asleep in their beds at the Hanslbauer Hotel.
Röhm had even left his bodyguard in Munich. There was carousing, Shirer records, but no plotting.
The plane landed in Munich at four in the morning. Hitler stormed into the Ministry of the Interior.
He walked up to an S.A. general and personally tore the insignia off his uniform, screaming traitor.
Then the column of cars set off for Wiessee, and for Röhm.
Shortly after dawn they reached the hotel. The awakening, Shirer writes, was rude.
In one room they found Edmund Heines, a convicted murderer, in bed with a young man.
Heines and his companion were dragged outside and shot on the spot, on Hitler's order.
Hitler walked into Röhm's room, gave his old friend a dressing-down, and ordered him to Stadelheim prison.
The same prison where Röhm had served time beside Hitler after the failed Beer Hall Putsch, eleven years before.
And so we come back to that cell, and that pistol on the table, and Röhm's refusal.
When the ten minutes passed, two S.S. officers entered. Röhm, stripped to the waist, tried to speak.
The S.S. man told him to shut up. Then they shot him point-blank. He died with his face full of contempt.
But Wiessee was only the beginning. In Berlin, Göring and Himmler had unleashed the lists.
At the Cadet School in Lichterfelde, 150 storm troopers were lined against a wall and cut down by firing squads.
Among them Karl Ernst, the Berlin S.A. leader, dragged from his honeymoon, shouting Heil Hitler to the end.
But the guns did not stop at the S.A. S.S. men rang the doorbell of General von Schleicher.
When Schleicher opened his own front door, they shot him dead. His wife stepped forward — they shot her too.
Gregor Strasser, once the second man in the party, was seized and shot in his cell on Göring's order.
Papen survived only by luck, under house arrest, while the S.S. gutted his office and murdered his staff.
Then the old grudges. Gustav von Kahr, who crushed the 1923 putsch, was found in a swamp, hacked to death.
A priest who once helped edit Mein Kampf was found in a forest, his neck broken, three bullets in his heart.
And a music critic named Willi Schmid was taken from his cello while his children played — killed by mistake for a man with a similar name.
Was there ever a plot at all? Shirer's verdict is unambiguous: there was not a shred of evidence.
The whole justification was manufactured, and the men who could contradict it were dead within the week.
Most of the killing was over by Sunday. And how did Hitler spend that afternoon? He hosted a tea party at the Chancellery.
The next day President Hindenburg sent his thanks, for nipping treason in the bud.
The cabinet passed a law declaring the entire massacre legal. And the Army — the Army said thank you.
They had no idea what they had done to themselves. On July 13th, Hitler stood before the Reichstag and said it out loud.
In this hour I was responsible for the fate of the German people, and thereby I became the supreme judge.
He had killed without trial, without evidence, without law — and had it ratified as law.
Then a promise: everyone must know that if he raises his hand against the State, certain death is his lot.
The reward: on July 26th the S.S. was made independent of the S.A., under Himmler, answerable only to Hitler.
Ten years later, almost to the day, when those same officers finally raised their hands against him, their bodies hung on meat hooks.
The Night of the Long Knives taught a nation that there was no law but one man's will — and the price of forgetting it was death.
